articles.title: France is rioting over surging inflation, skyrocketing national debt, and crumbling schools. America is its sleeping twin
articles.summary: Growth is the main thing keeping the U.S. from looking like France. Underneath it, the debt math and the classrooms look a lot alike.
articles.body:
The fire that badly damaged Limoges' 19th-century city hall was set on purpose, the local prefect said. By Sunday it was under control, and France was counting the damage: more than 2,400 arrests on Saturday alone , according to authorities, nearly 1,000 police and gendarmes injured, and hundreds of businesses looted in Paris, Marseille, Lyon, and other cities. Looting and fires continued Sunday night, and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu ordered localized curfews Monday. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez admitted police "lost control" and offered to resign. President Emmanuel Macron refused.

America has worse inflation, as Fortune 's Jason Ma reported Monday . U.S. consumer prices rose 3.7% in the year through September, compared with France's 3.4% on the EU-harmonized measure . What offsets it is growth. U.S. GDP rose 2.2% in the second quarter; unemployment is 4.2%; and wages are growing about 3.0% a year, below inflation. Meanwhile, France expects its economy to grow just 0.5% this year, and youth unemployment there is about 20%.

Set aside growth, and the two countries have a lot in common. And Americans aren't thrilled about where the growth is coming from. Tech investment accounts for about a third of U.S. GDP growth, according to ING . Yet 39% of Americans now say AI does more harm than good, up from 31% a year ago, and 79% expect AI to cut U.S. jobs over the next decade, according to a Bentley-Gallup survey conducted in May. Among adults under 30, the harm figure is 47%. A Pew survey in June found 52% of Americans more concerned than excited about AI.

Start with the debt. French public debt sits at a record 119% of GDP, while U.S. debt held by the public reached 100.2% of GDP at the end of March. Lecornu's budget, which would cut France's deficit to 5% of GDP from 5.4%, faces its first critical vote in the National Assembly on Tuesday. Washington ran a $1.992 trillion deficit in fiscal 2026, about 6.2% of GDP based on CBO's projections . Needless to say, that's wider than the 5.4% deficit France is rioting over.

Bond traders are treating the two countries alike. Bank of America economists Claudio Irigoyen and Antonio Gabriel recently found that the French and U.S. 10-year yields have been moving on nearly the same track, and they say the cause is the same. "When interest rates are low, governments have incentives to run bigger deficits financed with cheap debt," they wrote in a BofA Global Research report. "However, if that 'cheap' debt goes to finance a structural increase of the fiscal deficit, when interest rates increase it is politically difficult to implement the necessary fiscal consolidation to put the house in order."

articles.title: TCU aprova contas do Banco Central após impasse sobre Banco Master | G1
articles.standfirst: Decisão dos ministros de condicionar análise seguiu recomendação do Ministério Público junto ao TCU (MPTCU) e contrariou entendimento da área técnica do tribunal.
articles.summary: O TCU aprovou as contas do Banco Central de 2025, revertendo a decisão de condicionar a análise à conclusão do processo de liquidação do Banco Master.
articles.body:
Dias depois de condicionar o julgamento das contas do Banco Central à conclusão de um processo sobre a liquidação do Banco Master, o Tribunal de Contas da União (TCU) voltou atrás nesta terça-feira (20) e aprovou as contas da autoridade monetária referentes a 2025.

O TCU entendeu que as conclusões desse processo podem influenciar a análise das contas do BC e, por isso, decidiu aguardar uma decisão definitiva sobre o caso antes de concluir o julgamento das contas.

A posição dos ministros seguiu a recomendação do Ministério Público junto ao TCU (MPTCU) e contrariou o entendimento da área técnica do tribunal.

Na decisão desta terça, os ministros da Segunda Câmara do TCU determinaram o levantamento da suspensão que impedia a conclusão do julgamento. Com isso, as contas dos responsáveis foram consideradas regulares, com quitação plena, e o processo foi arquivado.

O acórdão cita a avaliação do MPTCU, segundo a qual “os elementos constantes dos autos não evidenciam irregularidades capazes de comprometer a regularidade das contas”.

O documento também registra que a posição do Ministério Público é convergente com a análise da área técnica do tribunal, favorável à aprovação das contas.

A análise da liquidação do banco tramita em outro processo, relatado pelo ministro Jhonatan de Jesus. O julgamento das contas do BC foi relatado pelo ministro Jorge Oliveira.

O tensionamento entre o Banco Central e o TCU começou no fim do ano passado, quando o ministro Jhonatan de Jesus determinou que a autoridade monetária apresentasse, em 72 horas, esclarecimentos sobre supostos indícios de que a liquidação do Banco Master teria ocorrido de forma "precipitada". O ministro também decretou sigilo sobre o processo.

Dias depois, no auge do atrito entre os órgãos, Jhonatan determinou uma inspeção nos documentos do BC por considerar que ainda faltavam informações para embasar as explicações apresentadas pela autoridade monetária sobre a liquidação, decretada em novembro.

O Banco Central recorreu. Argumentou que a inspeção não poderia ser determinada individualmente pelo relator e deveria ser submetida ao colegiado do TCU.

Jhonatan acolheu o pedido para levar a discussão sobre a inspeção ao plenário, mas contestou o argumento apresentado pelo BC.

"Sob o ângulo regimental, não procede a premissa de que a inspeção dependeria, necessariamente, de autorização exclusiva de órgão colegiado", afirmou o ministro à época.

Jhonatan também disse que a decisão de submeter o assunto ao plenário levou em consideração a "dimensão pública" alcançada pelo caso.

Em meio a isso, um parecer da equipe técnica do TCU em fevereiro já afastava a existência de irregularidades ou omissões na atuação do Banco Central no processo de liquidação do Master.

"Concluiu-se, ao final, que não foram identificadas impropriedades, omissões ou negligência na atuação do Banco Central do Brasil . A decretação da liquidação extrajudicial foi considerada medida imperativa, legal e tecnicamente fundamentada, adotada tempestivamente após o esgotamento fático das alternativas de recuperação e diante da insolvência e da possível prática de ilícitos pela instituição supervisionada", diz o parecer dos técnicos envolvidos na auditoria.

Banco Master — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Em março, Jhonatan de Jesus suspendeu a análise da atuação do Banco Central na liquidação extrajudicial do Banco Master até a conclusão de outras investigações relacionadas ao caso.

Na ocasião, o ministro afirmou que aguardar os demais procedimentos permitiria ao tribunal decidir com um conjunto mais completo de informações.

“Entendo que a apreciação imediata do relatório de inspeção e do mérito da representação, neste momento processual, não se afigura a medida mais adequada, sob pena de o julgamento ocorrer com grau de completude inferior ao desejável, quando há perspectiva concreta de superveniência de elementos oficiais aptos a qualificar o juízo definitivo”, afirmou o ministro.

articles.title: Home contract signings plunged in September amid higher mortgage rates
articles.summary: Home contract activity plunged in September as mortgage rates rose.
articles.body:
Housing contract signings dropped steeply in September as rapidly rising mortgage rates spooked would-be buyers .

Pending home sales, a measure of homes going under contract, fell 7.3% in September from a month earlier and 11.3% from a year ago, hitting their lowest levels since at least 2001, according to National Association of Realtors data released on Tuesday.

Mortgage rates rocketed from around 6.7% to near 7.5% over the course of September, further slowing an already-sluggish housing market. Economists had been bracing for slower contract activity last month, but the decline was far steeper than the 0.5% month-over-month drop and the 3.9% annual decline they had forecast.

"Market conditions weakened in September due to fast-rising mortgage rates," NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement. "Although job growth and income gains can support home purchases, housing affordability is more affected by changes in mortgage rates."

No part of the country was immune to the drop, but the smallest annual declines in pending home sales occurred in both the weakest and strongest housing markets. Buyer-friendly markets like Nashville and Austin, Texas, saw pending home sales drop 2% and 5.9%, respectively. In ultracompetitive Hartford, Conn., pending sales were down 2.1%, followed by a 3.5% decline in San Francisco and a 4.6% drop in San Jose, Calif. Pending home sales declined the most in Virginia Beach, Va., with a nearly 20% drop. In Louisville, Ky., they fell 15.8%, followed by Denver's 15.5% decline. Homes typically go under contract a month or two before they're sold, making pending home sales an early indicator of future sales activity. Claire Boston is a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance covering housing, mortgages, and home insurance.

articles.title: US food importer sues Trump over 50 percent tariffs on Canadian goods
articles.summary: The lawsuit argues Trump bypassed Congress and misused a Depression-era law to impose tariffs on Canadian imports.
articles.body:
A US food importer is suing US President Donald Trump over his 50 percent tariffs on Canadian goods, arguing he lacks the legal authority to impose sweeping tariffs without congressional approval.

Gellert Global Group, a New Jersey-based company that imports Canadian cheese, filed the lawsuit on Tuesday in the US Court of International Trade in New York.

The company says the tariffs are driving up its costs and disrupting its relationships with suppliers on both sides of the border. Between September 16 and October 11, Gellert had paid more than $520,000 in duties, according to the complaint .

“Gellert Global Group has spent generations building trusted relationships with suppliers, customers and partners across the food industry,” said Thomas Gellert, the company’s co-chief executive officer, in a press release . “These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain.”

The lawsuit challenges Trump’s decision to use a Depression-era law to impose tariffs on a wide range of Canadian products, including dairy products, furniture, clothing and wine.

Trump first imposed the 50 percent tariffs over the summer , accusing Canada of discriminating against American-made cars, alcohol and dairy products. He expanded the measures in September, adding more products in response to Canadian retaliatory tariffs .

The lawsuit argues that the law doesn’t apply to the Canadian policies the Trump administration says are discriminatory, since two of them “arose in response to the president’s own tariffs, while the third involves Canadian dairy policy governed by the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA)”.

It also questions why Canadian cheese is being taxed over disputes involving alcohol and cars.

“No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required,” said Sara Albrecht, chairman and CEO of the Liberty Justice Center, a nonprofit legal organisation that filed the suit on Gellert’s behalf.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment, according to the Reuters news agency.

At the centre of the case is Section 338 of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930, which allows the president to impose tariffs of up to 50 percent on imports from countries found to discriminate against American businesses.

The provision had never been used until Trump invoked it this year.

The lawsuit argues that newer laws passed by Congress since then, such as Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, require investigations, public comment and other safeguards that Gellert says the Trump administration has bypassed, and that these override Section 338.

“The administration cannot skip those protections by reaching for a 1930 statute that no president had ever used to impose a tariff,” said Jeffrey Schwab, the Liberty Justice Center’s senior counsel and director of litigation.

In addition, the lawsuit says that even if Trump is allowed to use the older law, he hasn’t met its requirements, including waiting 30 days before tariffs can be collected on new products added to the list.

The administration only waited seven days to start collecting tariffs on cheese in September, according to the lawsuit.

Gellert is asking the court to declare the tariffs illegal, stop them from being collected, and order refunds with interest for importers who have been impacted.

The lawsuit marks the fourth major legal challenge to Trump’s tariffs.

In February, the US Supreme Court struck down most of the tariffs he imposed in 2025, and a trade court later ruled against a temporary 10 percent global tariff. A separate challenge to tariffs imposed over alleged forced labour in international trade is still pending.

articles.title: Asean emerges as fastest growing region for exports
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: It all boils down to one commodity: Oil products.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: It all boils down to one commodity: Oil products. Asean has emerged as the fastest growing region for India’s exports due to a spurt in petro product shipments – mainly to Singapore -- while the European Union saw the slowest pace of increase during AprilAug as export of petroleum products fell.Latest data available with the commerce department showed that India’s exports to Asean went up 56% during the first five months of the fiscal year as oil product shipments soared 2.4 times to over $6.1 billion, with Singapore accounting for almost threefourths of it. What also helped was a 20-fold jump in computer hardware to $1.4 billion to Asean countries and strong growth of electric machinery (82% to $1.6 billion) and buffalo meat (42% to $1 billion)Since March, countries have recalibrated their energy purchases due to the disruption in West Asia.In contrast, when it comes to EU, oil product exports fell 21% to $4.6 billion as the Netherlands cut back on purchases from India. While the Netherlands was the top destination for Indian fuel, with exports of $5.3 billion during April-Aug 2025, it has now slipped to the third place, behind Singapore and Tanzania, as the value of shipments crashed 47% to $2.8 billion.A part of the impact in EU was offset by Spain and Italy. In April-Aug, India’s exports to Spain rose 54% to $3.5 billion, with oil products jumping to $1.1 billion during the period, as against $172 million ayear ago – an over six-fold increase. In case of Italy, the jump was even more dramatic as petroleum product exports rose from $4 million during April-Aug 2025 to $659 million so far this year.Oil exports to North America fell 7% to $1.9 billion and the 8% rise in overall exports to the region, largely the US, was led by iPhones as telecom instruments rose 29% to over $11 billion, accounting for 23.5% of the exports to the region. Pharma exports too fell 5% to just under $4 billion.Exports to the region slowed as the value of shipments to the US was up just over 6% to $42.8 billion, data showed.You use AI every day. articles.title: PE-VC investments shine, may exceed $39 billion this year
articles.summary: CHENNAI: Despite ongoing geopolitical disruptions, India’s private equity and venture capital (PE-VC) continues to rise.
articles.body: CHENNAI: Despite ongoing geopolitical disruptions, India’s private equity and venture capital (PE-VC) continues to rise. It is expected to exceed last year’s levels of $39 billion, signalling a consecutive YoY revival. International PE investors’ growing interest in Indian firms is putting greater focus on hard-asset businesses such as infrastructure and domestic manufacturing.Data sourced by TOI from research firm Venture Intelligence shows that investments to the tune of $39 billion, comprising 1,434 deals, were recorded in CY2025. With 1,076 deals, it has already reached $32.7 billion during the nine-month period (Jan-Sept, 2026). It was primarily driven by record PEVC investments in Sept 2026 at $6 billion. The PE-VC investments do not include those related to the real estate sector.“Based on the very strong Jul-Sept quarter investment figures, the PE-VC investment tally for 2026 can be expected to end the year at an amount similar to or higher than the previous year,” Arun Natarajan, founder of Venture Intelligence, said.After a plunge in PE-VC investments, which dropped to $48.9 billion in CY2022 from $64.4 billion in CY2021, it further decreased to $33.8 billion and $33.5 billion during CY2023 and CY2024, respectively. However, it revived last year (CY2025).Noting that the Indian economy has been able to withstand many external shocks, including an oil-price-impacting US-Iran war, he said the IPO market has also held up—despite volatility in the secondary markets. “One of the key highlights this year is PE investors doubling down on their infrastructure investments. Large foreign investors have made several mega bets on infrastructure companies across sectors like renewable energy, telecom towers & data centers and toll roads; especially dominant has been the role of Canadian investors—like La Caisse (formerly CDPQ), CPP Investments and Brookfield—who have deployed over $3 billion in infrastructure companies in 2026,” he added.Aniket Dharamshi, co-founder and managing partner, ValueQuest Investment Advisors, said headline investment numbers in 2026 could exceed last year’s levels, particularly if large infrastructure transactions sustain the momentum seen in the third quarter. “While India offers global investors an opportunity to diversify across sectors and growth drivers, beyond the concentration of capital in a few global technology themes, whether this translates into a higher deployment on core PE-VC will depend on economic and earnings growth, valuation expectations and a more stable investment environment,” he said.Geopolitics, national security, import substitution and supply-chain resilience are bringing greater strategic importance to businesses with tangible assets and domestic manufacturing capabilities. “At the same time, the AI build-out is creating demand from data centre infrastructure to power. Together, these forces are influencing where private capital is being deployed,” he added.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Smartphone shipments slip, Chinese brands lose ground
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India’s smartphone data entries hone market suffered its steepest contraction in several quarters, with shipments plunging 26% in July–Sept as
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India’s smartphone data entries hone market suffered its steepest contraction in several quarters, with shipments plunging 26% in July–Sept as higher prices put buyers off upgrades and prompted manufacturers to curb supplies ahead of the festive season.Shipments fell to 35.8 million units, the lowest third-quarter volume since 2016, according to Omdia. The slump also changed the pecking order: Samsung displaced Vivo at the top, while Chinese brands’ combined share slipped to about 68% from 75% a year earlier.Samsung shipped 6.7 million phones to regain leadership for the first time since early 2024. Its affordable Galaxy A-series supported volumes, while cashback, exchanges and longer financing plans helped attract buyers across price brackets.Vivo’s shipments dropped 34% to 6.4 million — the sharpest decline among the top five. Repeated price increases disrupted retailers’ inventory planning, while limited supplies of entry-level phones weakened its position. Xiaomi’s traditional appeal of offering more features for the money also came under pressure.Rising component costs forced trade-offs on pricing and memory configurations, with shipments falling 28% to 4.7 million. OPPO ranked third with 4.9 million units, down 24%. Apple took fifth place with 3.9 million phones. Demand for the iPhone 16 and base iPhone 17, along with stocking ahead of anticipated price increases, supported shipments.“Fewer exclusive launches, limited affordable SKUs and narrowing promotional differences reduced the online channel’s traditional festive advantage,” said Omdia principal analyst Sanyam Chaurasia.A later Diwali exaggerated the quarterly fall by shifting some offline festive stocking into Oct. The figures track supplies to sellers, rather than purchases by consumers. But, the weakness could persist beyond the festive calendar.Omdia expects another low-single-digit decline in 2027, with pricing pressure lasting through at least first half as consumers hold on to phones longer.You use AI every day. articles.title: Hacker group claims access to 3.8 lakh SBI data entries
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: An unidentified hacker group operating under the name ‘Siriusim’ has claimed to have obtained confidential customer information allegedly
articles.body: NEW DELHI: An unidentified hacker group operating under the name ‘Siriusim’ has claimed to have obtained confidential customer information allegedly linked to State Bank of India, including personal details, loan applications and account-opening documents.The claim was highlighted by cybersecurity monitoring account CyberPulse56 in a post on social media platform X. According to the account, the group purportedly possesses about 3.8 lakh data entries in CSV format and 2,722 pdf documents associated with the country’s largest public sector lender.The allegedly exposed dataset is said to contain customers’ personal information, residential addresses, loan applications, supporting documents and other applicationrelated records. CyberPulse56 first reported the claim on Oct 16, stating that Siriusim had presented the material as its first disclosure of the dataset.However, the authenticity and origin of the alleged data exposure remain unverified. The reported number of entries also does not establish how many individual customers may have been affected, as multiple records could potentially relate to the same person. There has been no independent confirmation that SBI’s systems were compromised or that the documents originated directly from the bank. CyberPulse56 warned that if the dataset proves genuine, the information could potentially be exploited for identity theft, financial fraud, targeted phishing attacks and fraudulent loan applications.The allegation comes amid broader concerns over cybersecurity risks facing India’s financial sector. Meanwhile, earlier this year, RBI stepped up cybersecurity requirements for commercial banks.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Hotel tariffs in Delhi, Mumbai top Rishikesh, Ranthambore
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: For the first time since Covid, the leisure and spiritual destinations — Ranthambore and Rishikesh — have been overtaken by Mumbai and Delhi as
articles.body: NEW DELHI: For the first time since Covid, the leisure and spiritual destinations — Ranthambore and Rishikesh — have been overtaken by Mumbai and Delhi as the Indian cities with highest average hotel tariffs. Leading hospitality consulting firm Hotelivate’s recently released trends & opportunities report for 2026 shows average revenue per available room (RevPAR) for Delhi at Rs 9,811; Mumbai Rs 9,761; Ranthambore Rs 9,649 and Rishikesh Rs 9,583 in FY 2025-26.In the previous fiscal, the top four positions were Ranthambore (Rs 0,059), Rishikesh (Rs 9,493), Mumbai (Rs 9,458) and Delhi (Rs 8,846).This shows a revival in corporate travel, international visitation and the group-oriented Meetings, Incentives, Conferences, and Exhibitions (MICE) activity. Varanasi has shown a big jump in average tariffs with the holy city boasting of the fifth highest rates at Rs 8,857 — ahead of Udaipur (Rs 8,414) and Goa (Rs 7,614) — in FY26, up from the ninth spot in previous fiscal when its RevPAR was Rs 6,769.The deadly Pahalgam terror attack last April saw Srinagar register its biggest fall in visitors. “Srinagar recorded the sharpest decline across the dataset, with RevPAR falling 51.9% year-on-year (to Rs 3,323 in FY 26) and the market moving from among the country’s leading performers to the bottom 15. Jalandhar, Jammu and Amritsar faced similar pressures, as cancellations associated with Operation Sindoor weakened demand across markets closer to the border,” says the report.“In recent years, leisure destinations, particularly emerging markets with limited supply and demand from destination weddings, (had) risen sharply in the national rankings. In 2025-26, however, Delhi and Mumbai emerged as the country’s leading RevPAR markets.… Leisure destinations such as Ranthambore, Rishikesh and Udaipur nevertheless remained among the top performers,” said the report.“The gap at the top also narrowed considerably, with less than Rs 250 separating the four leading markets, compared with a much wider spread in the previous year. Strong performance in these leisure destinations has attracted additional mid-market and upper midmarket supply, resulting in some normalisation in market-wide rates without displacing them from the country’s leading RevPAR markets,” it added.At the end of March 2026, India had a pipeline of 1.6 lakh hotel rooms to open in next five years. This was a 41% jump from the pipeline of 1.1 lakh exactly a year ago. “The pipeline is now approaching the scale of the country’s existing branded inventory. If it materialises in full, India’s branded hotel inventory would increase by 77% to approximately 3.7 lakh rooms. The top five markets are likely to be relatively unchanged with one exception; Jaipur is likely to surpass Chennai to become the fifth largest market in the country by operating inventory,” it said.You use AI every day. articles.title: SpaceX and Tesla have formed committees to discuss potential merger, Musk says
articles.summary: Elon Musk, the CEO of both SpaceX and Tesla, voiced support for merging the two companies during an earnings call Tuesday, though he said it is ultimately up to special shareholder committees from each company.
articles.body: Elon Musk, the CEO of both SpaceX and Tesla, voiced support for merging the two companies during an earnings call Tuesday, though he said it is ultimately up to special shareholder committees from each company. Asked about the long-rumored merger, Musk replied, “this is definitely kind of a question where I feel like I’m tap dancing through a minefield… but I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies.” The comments appeared to be the most forceful Musk has made publicly. When asked about the potential deal following SpaceX’s blockbuster July IPO, Musk didn’t offer an opinion one way or another, saying “obviously… we can’t talk about combining companies and that kind of thing on an earnings call. It’s got to be done with the appropriate process.” Musk on Tuesday was careful to manage investors’ expectations about any potential merger. As a “conflicted party,” he said, he cannot be a part of the discussions, noting the decision would be up to shareholders. Historically, Tesla shareholders have broadly fallen in line with Musk’s wishes, however. SpaceX shares rose nearly 5% in late trading, following its third-quarter earnings report that blew past Wall Street’s expectations. Tesla shares rose a little over 1%. The rocket, satellite internet, social media and AI company brought in net income of $4.4 billion in the most recent quarter, swinging to a profit after back-to-back quarters of losses this year. In its second earnings report since going public, SpaceX said it brought in $14.6 billion — up 161% year-over-year, according to the company, driven by what it called its “Super Intelligence” segment and its Starlink satellite-internet business. Wall Street analysts surveyed by FactSet had expected net income of $1.57 billion, with revenue of $12.9 billion. SpaceX reported earnings per share of 35 cents Tuesday, versus 14 cents forecast by analysts. Ukraine questions cloud SpaceX Moments before the earnings call Tuesday, the Wall Street Journal published a report saying that Musk “ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of Starlink” that blindsided Ukrainian officials. Musk during the call did not address the Journal report, which cited unnamed people familiar with the matter. CNN couldn’t immediately verify the veracity of the report. SpaceX didn’t immediately respond to CNN’s request for comment. Ukraine accused SpaceX last week of severely hindering its defense by suddenly limiting its Starlink internet service, which uses satellites in low orbit. Ukraine has used Starlink and a related military-grade service, Starshield, to communicate quickly and to both launch and prevent drone attacks. While Musk repeatedly suggested the White House was to blame for the disruption, the Trump administration has denied responsibility. On X, Musk emphasized that Starshield was “owned and controlled by the US government” and that “any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.”

articles.title: Review of 2019 mineral policy on cards amid new priorities
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Centre is set to review the National Mineral Policy, 2019, to align it with evolving sector demands, focusing on key priorities such as
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Centre is set to review the National Mineral Policy, 2019, to align it with evolving sector demands, focusing on key priorities such as critical minerals, recycling, and deep-sea resources, according to people in the know.The mines ministry has decided to constitute a panel to undertake a comprehensive review of the policy in the light of recent developments and emerging requirements. The nine-member committee will be chaired by the additional secretary in the mines ministry, they said. The panel has been asked to submit its recommendations within two months of its constitution.The National Mineral Policy, 2019, was approved by the Union cabinet chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. It was aimed at ensuring more effective regulation and sustainable development of the mining sector, and addressing the concerns of project-affected persons, particularly those living in tribal areas.The policy sought to create a more effective, meaningful and implementable framework by bringing in greater transparency, better regulation and enforcement, balanced social and economic growth, and sustainable mining practices. It also included provisions to boost the mining sector, such as measures to encourage exploration, attract private investment, promote ease of doing business and ensure sustainable mining.You use AI every day. articles.title: Spanberger pushes for 6-year rate-hike freeze if Dominion-Next Era merger approved
articles.summary: Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D) is pushing for a six-year pause on electricity rate hikes in the commonwealth as part of a merger between NextEra Energy and Dominion Energy. Spanberger on Monday filed expert testimony with the State Corporation Commission (SCC), urging it to reject the proposed merger if the two companies do not agree…
articles.body:
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D) is pushing for a six-year pause on electricity rate hikes in the commonwealth as part of a merger between NextEra Energy and Dominion Energy.

Spanberger on Monday filed expert testimony with the State Corporation Commission (SCC), urging it to reject the proposed merger if the two companies do not agree to halt increases to base electricity rates for six years — three rate case cycles.

Dominion, which is headquartered in Richmond, Va., and NextEra announced plans to merge in May. The deal would create the world’s largest regulated electric utility business by market capitalization, the companies said at the time.

Under the deal, which the two companies said in May they expect to close in 12 to 18 months, NextEra will acquire Dominion for nearly $67 billion in equity.

The two companies have said customers in North Carolina, South Carolina and Virginia would receive $2.25 billion in shareholder-funded bill credits upon closing.

But Spanberger outlined her stipulations for the deal to go through, calling on the companies to triple the ratepayer benefits to Virginians, which would increase the rebate to $29 per month for four years.

The first-year Virginia governor, who campaigned on lowering the cost of living, clarified Tuesday that her proposal would allow for electricity rates to decrease if economic conditions warrant.

“In the event that rates would otherwise be going down, there could be a review by the SCC that would … revisit that pricing if it’s going down,” Spanberger told reporters on a press call.

Virginia’s average residential electricity rate is 17.55 cents per kilowatt-hour (kWh), below the national average of 18.31 cents per kWH, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration .

Spanberger acknowledged Tuesday that SCC commissioners are “still a ways away” from deciding whether to greenlight the NextEra-Dominion merger. But she said the deal “is not nearly good enough” for Virginians.

“I am going to make clear the very long, very clear and … I would call it aggressive, but also quite realistic, requirements that I think would be necessary to meet for this potential merger to actually meet the stated benefits for Virginians,” the Virginia governor added.

articles.title: Classrooms to customers: What student founders need
articles.summary: BENGALURU: Classrooms have been carved out of office space inside a WeWork building on Bannerghatta Road in Bengaluru.
articles.body: BENGALURU: Classrooms have been carved out of office space inside a WeWork building on Bannerghatta Road in Bengaluru. A postgraduate timetable runs from noon to 8 pm, fitting study blocks around time for building businesses. Shrey Doshi (25), a postgraduate alumnus, walks in with a blue drink. “That’s my product. Try it,” he says, before explaining the blue spirulina and tender coconut.This is Mesa School of Business, where students must build businesses and find paying customers. Elsewhere, engineering clubs and laboratories offer another route into entrepreneurship. Across campuses, the support founders need ranges from time away from classes to equipment, early funding and introductions to buyers.“The clearest difference comes from two things: time to build and access to infrastructure,” said Richa Bajpai of Campus Fund, which invests in student-led businesses. She cited BITS Pilani’s attendance flexibility and option to take time off to build as reasons it remained among the leading institutions supplying pitches to her fund. “Students who start companies still face rigid exam schedules and attendance rules that force a choice between their degree and their company,” she said.Colleges also need to let students learn across disciplines, she added. For technical businesses, support can be tangible. IIT Jammu gave MachFly Aerospace labs, resources and early financial support to build its first prototype, Bajpai said. Incubators also give young companies access to equipment they could not afford themselves, professors with domain expertise and alumni with industry experience, she said.Bajpai points to govt grants, competitions and cloud credits as starting points for founders without family money or business connections. She also cited Human Biogenesis, whose founders came from humble backgrounds and started at BioNEST, IIT Guwahati’s incubator.The company has since completed clinical trials, raised aseed round and is moving into production, she said. At IIT Madras, director V Kamakoti described Centre for Innovation as “run by the student for the student”. Design clubs can feed into prototype development, with incubators, faculty and alumni supporting student teams. Citing Ather Energy’s journey, he spoke of “12 to 13 years of gestation” and the need for patient capital.Other businesses can test demand sooner. Campus Fundbacked Mumbai Pav Co began with Mesa classmates Tanay Agarwal and Jash Arora making food in another operator’s kitchen and selling to business customers before opening a store, Agarwal said. He already knew his family’s restaurant businesses; Arora brought culinary training. Access is uneven. Mesa’s advertised four-year undergraduate programme costs Rs 48 lakh, excluding accommodation and overseas immersions. It does not award a university degree.You use AI every day. articles.title: GCCs emerging top career choice for tech talent: Survey
articles.summary: BENGALURU: Indian technology professionals are increasingly looking for employers that offer hands-on artificial intelligence (AI) experience and clearly
articles.body: BENGALURU: Indian technology professionals are increasingly looking for employers that offer hands-on artificial intelligence (AI) experience and clearly defined career paths, while multinational global capability centres (GCCs) are emerging as the preferred next career move for many, according to a Talent500 survey. Talent500 is part of ANSR, which has set up more than 200 GCCs in India.Thesurvey of 2,000 technology, product and data professionals found that 71% wanted hands-on AI upskilling, but only 29% said their employers provided it. Career growth was another major concern: 87% said clearly defined career paths were very important when evaluating an employer, while 79% said they would abandon an application or decline an offer if growth opportunities were unclear.The gap is also visible in employees’ current workplaces. Only 46% of respondents described their career paths as very clear. Among GCC employees, the figure fell to 36%, compared with 50% in IT services and 51% in startups. This could make career clarity a differentiator for GCCs competing for experienced technology talent, particularly as candidates increasingly seek clarity on career progression before joining an employer.GCCs were the first choice for the next career move for 69% of respondents, ahead of Indian product companies at 37% and IT services and outsourcing firms at 28%. Career growth was the leading factor in evaluating a GCC, cited by 48%, followed by the global parent brand at 41%, India-centre leadership and culture at 36%, and exposure to AI and technology at 33%. Vikram Ahuja, co-founder of ANSR and CEO of 1Wrk, said GCC hiring was growing 15-18% annually, with roles changing rather than hiring coming to a halt.

articles.title: Elon Musk says SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss merger idea
articles.summary: Musk said he isn’t a member of either special committee or involved in the talks because he’s a conflicted party under securities regulations.
articles.body: Tech billionaire Elon Musk said Tuesday that the boards of SpaceX and Tesla had separately formed special committees to discuss the idea of a merger, taking a small step toward the possible consolidation of his two biggest companies. Musk, who is the CEO of both companies, said that the special committees had not reached an agreement and that there was no guarantee they would. He said a merger would require support from both sets of shareholders. “I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it,” he said. Musk spoke about the potential tie-up during a call with Wall Street analysts about SpaceX’s quarterly results, which surpassed estimates; the company’s revenue more than doubled in part from renting out computing capacity to other artificial intelligence firms. There has been intense speculation in the stock market over whether a combination might happen, and the two companies already overlap in some areas, including semiconductor manufacturing. In January, Tesla announced that it was investing about $2 billion to acquire shares in an AI startup that’s a subsidiary of SpaceX. Musk said that, because he’s a conflicted party under securities regulations, he is not a member of either special committee or involved in the talks. He said the committees consist of the two boards’ independent directors but did not specify the memberships. “It’s an odd Kabuki dance, where groups of people are talking and I can’t be in the conversation,” he said during the earnings calls. He also said that even answering a question about the idea from an analyst felt like “dancing through a minefield.” Musk, though, endorsed the idea. “I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies, as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there’s a lot to be gained from cooperating,” he said. He mentioned several areas of current or potential future cooperation, including AI software development, chip design and robotics. Musk has already consolidated some of his other holdings. Last year, he merged his social media company, X, with his AI startup, called at the time xAI. Then, in February, SpaceX acquired xAI, which Musk has since renamed SpaceXSI.

articles.title: NI universities face 'substantial' cuts amid budget delay
articles.summary: Both Queen's University Belfast and Ulster University are expected to have financial deficits in 2025/26.
articles.body:
Northern Ireland's universities are facing a "substantial" cut of £21m in the Stormont funding they receive to teach students.

The top official at the Department for the Economy (DfE), Ian Snowden, said the universities were facing a reduction of 6% on the opening funding they received in 2024/25.

The potential cuts come as the Northern Ireland Executive remains seven months into the financial year without a budget.

Snowden said both Queen's University Belfast (QUB) and Ulster University (UU) are expected to have financial deficits in 2025/26.

With no agreed budget for 2025/26, Stormont departments have been operating under contingency arrangements allowing them to spend up to 95% of last year's funding.

The DfE is the Stormont department with responsibility for higher and further education in Northern Ireland.

Universities are mainly funded through student fees and a "teaching grant" provided by DfE.

Further education colleges have already announced big cuts to student places and courses.

Ulster University, meanwhile, is making 450 staff redundant across its campuses to save about £25m.

'We don't know how much we have to spend'

The chair of Stormont's economy committee, Democratic Unionist Party assembly member Phillip Brett, said a further cut in university funding could mean that the universities would not receive money for three months for students they have already enrolled.

"The universities have taken students on in the anticipation that they will receive funding from the department," he said.

"We're now six months into the financial year and they still haven't received a formal letter of offer from the department.

"And despite students enrolling in September, one of the contingencies from the department is now that come January, February, March you might say 'actually we're not going to pay you for these three months of the students that you've taken on'?"

"It's a possibility," Snowden told the committee.

He also said the universities could only get confirmation of how much funding they would get when the executive agreed a budget.

"At this point we still don't know how much money we have to spend," he said.

Amy Smith, the National Union of Students-Union of Students in Ireland (NUS-USI) president, said it was "disappointing to hear that our universities will be facing cuts to their teaching grants".

"Any cuts directly impact students, their access to their education and the quality of the experience they receive while at university costs to them remain the same," she added.

"Students and staff must not be left to shoulder the cost of underfunding.

"We stand together in calling for the investment needed to protect jobs, access to education, and the quality of teaching."

A spokesperson for Queen's said the university was "operating in a challenging financial environment and has consistently highlighted that the current higher education funding model, and continued budget uncertainty, are unsustainable".

"We continue to work constructively with the Department for the Economy and government partners to secure a long-term solution that will benefit students and the wider economy," they said.

"Queen's continues to monitor the financial and funding environment closely and remains focused on managing resources responsibly to protect the university's long-term financial sustainability while continuing to deliver for our students, staff and wider society."

A spokesperson for Ulster University said it was "already enacting a substantial savings plan".

"Given the deteriorating funding situation from the department, which we regard as very serious, we will continue to enact appropriate caution in relation to our finances," the spokesperson said.

They also said 735 university staff had applied for voluntary redundancy.

articles.title: Netflix doesn’t want investors to worry, despite recent shake-ups, layoffs
articles.summary: “Reminder, we are a streaming-first business. That is our core,” co-CEO Ted Sarandos said on the streamer’s third-quarter earnings call.
articles.body: Following a dramatic C-suite reshuffle and its largest round of layoffs in years, Netflix’s top executives reassured investors Tuesday that they have a plan to keep audiences hooked. The streaming giant announced that its third-quarter revenue grew 12% year over year, to $12.9 billion, while net income rose 48%, to nearly $3.7 billion. “Our engagement is solid, and it will allow us to continue to grow as we have for the last several years,” co-CEO Greg Peters said on the streamer’s third-quarter earnings call, referring to the company’s performance in the U.S. “But we know that we can do better.” Revenue increased despite upheaval at Netflix, which last week laid off roughly 1,000 employees, or 6% of its workforce, and ousted Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria and top film executives Dan Lin and Doug Belgrad. “We believe we have a responsibility to make hard trade-offs in service of our members, our partners, our employees, our investors and ultimately our long-term growth,” Peters said of the layoffs. “That was the simple thinking behind it and what motivated these recent changes.” Over the last year, Netflix’s stock has dropped significantly, from $124.14 in October 2025 to $68.69 on Tuesday, because of slowing revenue growth. Netflix remains the biggest subscription streaming video service in the world, with more than 325 million global subscribers. But it has struggled to boost user engagement amid increasing competition from YouTube, despite expanding its push into live sports, video podcasts and gaming. Co-chief Ted Sarandos tapped former Disney and Fox executive Peter Rice to step into Bajaria’s role, telling investors and journalists that he “understands talent relations.” “In a competitive market, creative talent have choices of where they want to work, and we want Netflix to always be the place that they love to do the best work of their life,” Sarandos said. “Peter is the exact right person to lead those efforts in the U.S. and around the world. Now, that’s a key aspect of what I believe Peter can improve on looking forward.” Other major Hollywood studios are also trying to reduce costs and streamline operations. The Walt Disney Co. has cut hundreds of jobs this year under new CEO Josh D’Amaro, and David Ellison’s Skydance is expected to shrink its workforce across Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery. (In February, Netflix officially pulled out of a deal to buy WBD, ceding in a bidding war to Paramount.) Amid industry consolidation, Netflix reported slower revenue growth in the U.S. and Canada, where sales rose 11% in the third quarter, compared with 17% a year earlier. Still, in its letter to shareholders, it stressed that its strength lies in its “differentiated, exclusive, professionally produced series, films and live events.” It singled out the performances of recent programming, including “The Last House,” “Death of the Pastor’s Wife” and an NFL game in Australia. It also touted its upcoming slate of shows and movies, such as “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” a David Fincher-directed, Quentin Tarantino-written sequel to “Once Upon a Time... in Hollywood”; “The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey,” starring Melissa McCarthy and Clive Owen; new seasons of its popular shows “The Diplomat” and “Nobody Wants This”; three NFL games on Thanksgiving Eve and Christmas Day; and the Tyson Fury vs. Anthony Joshua fight. On the earnings call, Sarandos also discussed Netflix’s recent theatrical releases, including its first disclosure of box-office results for the Spanish-language Oscar contender “La bola negra,” and upcoming IMAX releases such as Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew.” “Reminder, we are a streaming-first business. That is our core,” he said. “We start off by looking at the projects we have, asking ourselves how do we best serve movie lovers, many of whom are our members who want to see that movie in a theater, and how do we do it without actually harming the view value to Netflix.”

Ted Sarandos, Peter Rice, Bela Bajaria and Dan Lin. Getty; WireImage

articles.title: Elon Musk says SpaceX-Tesla merger is a 'good idea', special committees formed for talks
articles.summary: Elon Musk’s business empire could be heading towards a major consolidation, with SpaceX and Tesla setting up special committees to discuss a possible
articles.body: Elon Musk’s business empire could be heading towards a major consolidation, with SpaceX and Tesla setting up special committees to discuss a possible merger. Musk confirmed the talks on Tuesday, saying he viewed combining the two companies favourably, although any deal would depend on the committees’ deliberations and approval from shareholders."I think it would be a good idea, but it's really up to the special committees of both companies," Musk said, in the first official confirmation that the companies were formally talking. "Because I'm a conflicted party, I can't actually be in the discussion of the special committees," he told investors on a conference call as per news agency Reuters. Shareholders ultimately would need to approve a deal, he added.SpaceX shares rose 4.9% in extended trading following the remarks. Speculation about a potential deal has grown in recent weeks, with Barclays suggesting last week that an announcement could come before Tesla's annual meeting in December. Musk has previously floated the idea, pointing to increasing overlap between the businesses.SpaceX posts first public-company profit as AI revenue surgesThe merger discussions came as SpaceX reported its first profit as a public company, alongside a sharp rise in revenue from artificial intelligence (AI). Revenue increased 161% year-on-year to $14.58 billion in the three months ended September 30.AI revenue surged almost tenfold to $7.56 billion, largely driven by renting data-centre computing capacity to developers such as Anthropic, Google's parent Alphabet and Reflection AI, rather than by sales from its own AI models."We are in an inflection moment for SpaceX across launch, connectivity and superintelligence," Musk said on the call. He ended his portion of prepared remarks with a seemingly off-script remark. "In a nutshell, what this implies for SpaceX annual recurring revenue by the end of '27 is somewhere between $500 billion and a trillion."SpaceX chief financial officer Bret Johnsen reiterated that the company expected annual recurring revenue of about $100 billion by the end of 2026. The company plans to spend $35 billion to $40 billion on capital expenditure in the fourth quarter. AI accounted for $16.4 billion of its $19.6 billion in capital spending in the third quarter, with investment in computing infrastructure nearly tripling.SpaceX reported net income of $4.4 billion, compared with a loss of $1.1 billion a year earlier. The result also beat analysts' average expectation of a $1.57 billion profit. On an adjusted per-share basis, the company earned 45 cents, above the average estimate of 13 cents, according to IBES calculations."SpaceX delivered the quarter the bulls wanted, at least on the top line," said Will Rhind, CEO of asset manager GraniteShares. "The story now is all about AI. The compute contracts signed earlier this year are turning into revenue faster than a lot of people thought."Starlink growth and Starship remain key to long-term plansSpaceX's expanding AI business includes Grok, social media platform X and its growing data-centre operations. However, the AI unit has incurred large operating losses, and the company has warned that sustained investment will be needed before it can generate consistent profits."With AI revenue now the company's biggest business line, the company's hyperscale business is quickly providing operating strength and leverage which will carry into the advancements of its satellite and launch business," said Daniel Newman, CEO of tech research group the Futurum Group. "Increasingly, the strength and diversification of SpaceX makes a merger with Tesla feel imminent."Starlink, SpaceX's satellite internet business, also continued to expand. It had 13.6 million subscribers in the third quarter, exceeding analysts' expectation of 12.19 million. However, average monthly revenue per subscriber fell from $99 in 2023 to $69 in the latest quarter as the company expanded into more markets with cheaper plans. SpaceX has warned that entering countries with lower purchasing power could push average revenue per user down further.The company's longer-term plans also depend on Starship, its next-generation reusable rocket system, which has yet to enter commercial service. The rocket is expected to help deploy more advanced Starlink satellites and support plans for AI computing infrastructure in orbit.SpaceX successfully deployed several Starlink satellites last month during Starship's first orbital test flight, although the flight ended hours earlier than expected following an engine issue. While Falcon rocket launches remain active across commercial and government missions, Starship development continues to involve significant costs and uncertainty.SpaceX has also increasingly prioritised launching satellites for its own network over carrying third-party payloads. The combination of a growing AI business, expanding satellite connectivity and ambitious rocket development has changed the company's financial profile, making the potential merger with Tesla a significant development for both businesses.(With inputs from Reuters)You use AI every day.
